newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania asks Italy to clarify resignation remark.
newsitem.headline: Albania asks Italy to clarify resignation remark.

text.p: Albania issued a strongly worded diplomatic protest to Italy's ambassador in Tirana on Tuesday after Rome's deputy foreign minister said the Italian government believed Albanian President Sali Berisha should leave office.

After first rejecting the remarks as an unacceptable interference into Albania's domestic affairs, Albania sent an even harsher diplomatic note to the Italian embassy in Tirana seeking immediate "clarification" of the comments.

"Albania's Foreign Ministry asks...for the Italian Foreign Ministry, before the adoption of any other decision, to clarify the position of the Italian government regarding the irresponsible statements of deputy Foreign Minister, Fassino," said the note released on the state ATA news agency.

The rebuke was handed to the embassy before the Italian parliament voted on Tuesday evening to approve government plans for Italian soldiers to lead a U.N.-backed peacekeeping force of some 6,000 soldiers, but was not made public until later.
Although Deputy Foreign Minister Piero Fassino stopped short of calling on Berisha to resign immediately, saying Italy would not push for him to quit now, his remarks were firmly rejected in Tirana.

"We energetically protest against this unacceptable interference in the internal affairs from the Italian Foreign Ministry..," said a first Foreign Ministry statement, released earlier on Tuesday, addressed to the Italian Foreign Ministry.
Both the protest note and the stronger second letter were handed to the Italian embassy in Tirana.
"The irresponsible statement only serves to divide and further destabilise the situation in Albania," said Berisha's spokesman in a statement released to journalists in Tirana on Tuesday evening.
"It is up to the Albanian people to decide who should be at the head of the constitutional institutions of the Albanian state."
More than 200 people have been killed and 700 injured in weeks of armed rampage that have swept Albania, Europe's poorest nation, since investment schemes collapsed earlier this year.
Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi, whose centre-left government has been badly split over Italy's plans to lead a peacekeeping mission to Albania, quickly distanced himself from Fassino's remarks.
"We are not going to Albania to interfere or get involved in the complex local situation," Prodi told the Italian Senate before the upper house voted on the mission.

"We are not going there to reaffirm who's on top or to safeguard partisan interests," he added. "We are going there to offer Albanians the concrete support they need so that they themselves, as is their responsibility, can restore conditions for normal life in their country through free elections."

Berisha, in office since 1992, has said he will resign if his party loses early general elections due to take place by the end of June under a broad political agreement reached last month to try to end his Balkan country's anarchy.
